title: DPP-4 inhibitor: increases glucose-dependent insulin release (via GLP-1)
vignette: A 56-year-old man comes to the office for follow-up of type 2 diabetes mellitus. The patient has had inadequate glycemic control with metformin monotherapy; an additional medication that inhibits dipeptidyl peptidase-4 was prescribed 3 months ago. The patient also has hypertension for which he takes ramipril. He does not use tobacco, alcohol, or recreational drugs. Blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg and pulse is 76/min. BMI is 31.4 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory results show a hemoglobin A1c of 6.8%. The newly prescribed medication most likely improved this patient's glycemic control through which of the following mechanisms?

clues.text: inadequate glycemic control with metformin monotherapy
clues.note: Add-on therapy after metformin is a common scenario; the specific drug class named determines the mechanism.
A DPP-4 inhibitor (e.g., sitagliptin) blocks the enzyme that degrades incretins (GLP-1), raising GLP-1 levels and enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

whatMatters: A DPP-4 inhibitor (a 'gliptin') blocks breakdown of the incretin GLP-1, raising its level. GLP-1 INCREASES GLUCOSE-DEPENDENT INSULIN RELEASE (and suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying). Answer D. Because the insulin effect is glucose-dependent, hypoglycemia risk is low.
strategy: Trace the incretin axis: DPP-4 normally degrades GLP-1; inhibiting DPP-4 -> more GLP-1 -> glucose-dependent insulin secretion up + glucagon down. Match to 'increased glucose-dependent insulin release.' Reject other drug-class mechanisms: acarbose (decreased carb digestion), SGLT2 inhibitor (decreased renal glucose reabsorption), and metformin/TZD (increased peripheral glucose uptake). GLP-1 SUPPRESSES glucagon (so 'increased glucagon' is wrong).

eliminations.label: Decreased carbohydrate digestion - alpha-glucosidase inhibitor
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: slowing intestinal carbohydrate breakdown (acarbose/miglitol). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: DPP-4 inhibitors don't affect carbohydrate digestion; they act via incretins. ✅ Correct if: acarbose (postprandial glucose control, GI side effects).

eliminations.label: Decreased renal glucose reabsorption - SGLT2 inhibitor
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: blocking proximal-tubule glucose reabsorption to cause glucosuria (canagliflozin/dapagliflozin). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that is the SGLT2-inhibitor mechanism, not a DPP-4 inhibitor. ✅ Correct if: an SGLT2 inhibitor (glucosuria, weight/BP benefit).

eliminations.label: Increased glucagon secretion - opposite of GLP-1 effect
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: raising glucagon (which would RAISE glucose). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: GLP-1 SUPPRESSES glucagon; DPP-4 inhibitors (by raising GLP-1) decrease glucagon, not increase it. ✅ Correct if: never for this class - it's the opposite effect.

eliminations.label: Increased peripheral glucose uptake - metformin/TZD (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: improving insulin sensitivity/peripheral glucose uptake (metformin, thiazolidinediones). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: DPP-4 inhibitors work by enhancing incretin-driven, glucose-dependent INSULIN SECRETION, not by increasing peripheral uptake. ✅ Correct if: metformin (AMPK) or a TZD (PPAR-gamma).

reasoning: DPP-4 normally degrades the incretin GLP-1
GLP-1 increases glucose-dependent insulin release (and suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying)
-> increased glucose-dependent insulin release; answer D
mechanism: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is an incretin released by intestinal L cells after a meal; it lowers glucose by increasing glucose-DEPENDENT insulin secretion, suppressing glucagon, slowing gastric emptying, and reducing appetite. GLP-1 is rapidly degraded by the enzyme dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4). DPP-4 INHIBITORS ('gliptins,' e.g., sitagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin) block this degradation, raising endogenous GLP-1 levels and thereby enhancing glucose-dependent insulin release and lowering hemoglobin A1c. Because the insulinotropic effect is glucose-dependent (insulin is secreted only when glucose is elevated), DPP-4 inhibitors carry a LOW risk of hypoglycemia as monotherapy - a key advantage. GLP-1 receptor agonists (exenatide, liraglutide) act on the same pathway more potently and are resistant to DPP-4. The distractor mechanisms belong to other classes: alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (decreased carb digestion), SGLT2 inhibitors (decreased renal glucose reabsorption), and metformin/thiazolidinediones (increased peripheral glucose uptake); raising glucagon is the opposite of GLP-1's action.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm/Endo > DPP-4 inhibitors ('-gliptins'): block GLP-1 breakdown -> ↑glucose-dependent insulin, ↓glucagon; low hypoglycemia risk; GLP-1 agonists similar but more potent.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: DPP-4 inhibition raises GLP-1 -> glucose-dependent insulin release (not peripheral uptake).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on incretin, GLP-1, DPP-4, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, or gliptin? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Acarbose (carb digestion), SGLT2 (renal glucose), metformin/TZD (peripheral uptake); GLP-1 lowers glucagon, so 'increased glucagon' is opposite.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: DPP-4 inhibitor -> ↑GLP-1 -> ↑glucose-dependent insulin + ↓glucagon; minimal hypoglycemia.

firstAid.detail: Pharm: ↑GLP-1 -> glucose-dependent insulin release; low hypoglycemia risk.
Endo > acarbose (carb digestion), SGLT2 (renal glucose), metformin/TZD (peripheral uptake).
Endo > GLP-1 from L cells; degraded by DPP-4; agonists resist DPP-4.

memoryHook: Gliptins guard GLP-1 from the DPP-4 shredder - more GLP-1 means insulin only when sugar's high, so glucose drops without hypoglycemia.
